en.title: Zoology: the whole course
en.short: What zoology covers, how zoology degrees are organised, and how to study the subject well.

sections.heading: What zoology is
sections.text:
Zoology is the scientific study of animals: their structure, how their bodies work, how they develop, how they behave, how they inherit traits, and how they interact with each other and with their surroundings. It is one branch of biology, alongside botany, the study of plants. Modern zoology works at every scale, from DNA and proteins to whole populations and ecosystems.

The subject matters for practical reasons. Animals are food, income and disease carriers. Fisheries, livestock, wildlife tourism and public health all depend on understanding them, and conservation depends on knowing how species respond when habitats change.

These notes teach principles and standard methods. They do not replace a laboratory manual, a field guide, a species checklist, or your country’s law on wildlife, animal welfare and research permits.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.

In Nigeria a BSc in zoology commonly takes four years at a university. The first year is largely biology, chemistry, mathematics and general studies; later years add zoology courses, laboratory and field work, and a final-year project. Many programmes include industrial training under SIWES, the Students Industrial Work Experience Scheme. Polytechnics offer National Diploma (ND) and Higher National Diploma (HND) awards in related science subjects rather than a BSc. The National Universities Commission sets benchmark standards, but departments vary.

In the UK a BSc usually takes three years (four in Scotland) and an integrated master’s such as an MSci usually four. In Ghana and Kenya a BSc commonly takes four years. A master’s adds advanced courses and a research dissertation; its length varies, so check the department.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text:
The course begins with tools and framework. Scientific method and biostatistics teach how to design an experiment, measure and analyse data. Biomolecules and cells, cell division and genetics, and evolution by natural selection supply the ideas. Classification and taxonomy show how animals are named and grouped, then surveys of invertebrate and vertebrate diversity follow. Animal form and function introduces tissues and homeostasis, and ecology and biomes place animals in their environments.

The core stage goes deeper. Anatomy and histology, comparative physiology, nutrition and metabolism, endocrinology and reproduction, developmental biology, neurobiology and immunology cover how bodies are built and run. Parasitology, entomology and animal behaviour apply this to real problems. Population and community ecology, conservation and wildlife management, phylogenetics, molecular biology and biotechnology, field methods, fisheries and aquaculture, and professional practice complete the core.

At master’s level come advanced evolutionary genomics, molecular ecology and conservation genetics, ecophysiology, and research methods leading to a dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Learn the vocabulary early. Terms such as homeostasis, homology, clade and taxon carry precise meanings, and later topics assume them.

Draw and label diagrams from memory: a neuron, a nephron, a fish gill, a grasshopper’s mouthparts. Then compare across groups. How does gas exchange work in a fish, an insect and a mammal, and why does it differ? Comparison is the heart of zoology.

Use specimens and field time properly. A dissection or a museum specimen teaches more than a photograph, and a labelled sketch you make yourself is better revision than a copied one. Keep a field notebook with date, place, weather and method.

For quantitative topics, work the calculations by hand. If a mark-recapture study marks 40 animals and a second sample of 50 contains 8 marked, the estimate is (40 × 50) ÷ 8 = 250. Check the assumptions before trusting that number.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Learning names without reasons. A list of phyla is useless unless you can say what defines each group and how it differs from its neighbours.

Confusing analogy with homology, and similarity with relatedness. A dolphin’s fin and a shark’s fin do similar jobs but are not inherited from the same ancestor in the same way.

Treating classification as fixed. Taxonomy changes as genetic evidence arrives, so learn the current scheme and expect revision.

Ignoring scale and statistics in ecology. A pattern seen in one pond in one season is not a general law.

Forgetting that physiology is about balance. Students describe what an organ does but not how the body holds a variable steady.

Careless practical work: unlabelled drawings, missing units, no control group, no record of method.

keyPoints: Zoology studies animals at every level, from molecules and cells to populations and ecosystems.
Degree length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
The course moves from tools and framework, through animal diversity, to body systems, ecology and applied fields.
Comparison across animal groups is the central skill: learn what defines each group, not just its name.
Draw diagrams from memory, work calculations by hand, and keep a proper field notebook.
These notes teach principles and do not replace laboratory manuals, field guides or your country’s wildlife and welfare law.

en.title: Scientific method, measurement and biostatistics in zoology
en.short: Hypotheses, sampling, descriptive statistics and introductory tests for zoological data.

sections.heading: Hypotheses and design
sections.text: A hypothesis is a testable explanation. It leads to a prediction: if the hypothesis is true, what should be observed? A good experiment changes one independent variable, measures the dependent variable, and holds other variables constant. Controls are untreated or standard groups; replication and random assignment reduce chance effects and confounding, where another variable masks the true cause. A pilot study checks methods before full work.

sections.heading: Measurement and sampling
sections.text: Measurement gives numbers meaning. Record units, calibrate instruments, and distinguish accuracy (closeness to true value) from precision (repeatability). Data are categorical or numerical. Sampling selects part of a population. Random sampling gives every individual a known chance of selection; systematic and stratified sampling are alternatives. Bias arises if some animals are more likely to be caught, so state sample size and method.

sections.heading: Describing data
sections.text: Descriptive statistics summarise. Mean = Σx ÷ n; median is the middle value; standard deviation (SD) measures spread. Standard error (SE) = SD ÷ √n estimates uncertainty of a mean. Probability describes chance. The p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as observed if the null hypothesis is true; it is not the probability that the hypothesis is true. By convention, many use p < 0.05, but this is a convention, not a law.

sections.heading: Tests and graphs
sections.text: A t-test compares two means. Chi-square tests association in categorical data or goodness of fit: chi-square = Σ (O − E)² ÷ E, with df = categories − 1 for goodness of fit. ANOVA compares three or more means. Example: observed phenotypes 30, 50, 20 against expected 1:2:1 (25, 50, 25). chi-square = (30−25)²÷25 + (50−50)²÷50 + (20−25)²÷25 = 1 + 0 + 1 = 2. With df = 2, the 5% critical value is 5.991, so do not reject. Graphs: bar charts for categories, scatter plots for two numerical variables, box plots for spread; label axes and units and avoid misleading scales.

keyPoints: A hypothesis must be testable and linked to a prediction; controls, replication and random assignment reduce confounding.
Mean = Σx ÷ n; standard deviation measures spread; standard error = SD ÷ √n.
A p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as observed if the null hypothesis is true, not the probability that the null is true.
A t-test compares two means; ANOVA compares three or more means.
Chi-square = Σ (O − E)² ÷ E for categorical data; for goodness of fit, df = categories − 1.
Choose graphs to match data type and label axes, units and sample size.

en.title: Biomolecules, cell structure and function
en.short: Water, carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, nucleic acids, cell types, organelles, membranes, transport and enzymes.

sections.heading: Biomolecules
sections.text: Water is polar and a good solvent; its high specific heat and cohesion help cells keep stable conditions. Carbohydrates are sugars and polymers such as starch, glycogen and cellulose; they store energy and give structure. Lipids are hydrophobic: fats store energy, phospholipids build membranes, and steroids act as signals. Proteins are chains of amino acids that fold into shapes; they act as enzymes, structural fibres and transporters. Nucleic acids are DNA and RNA, polymers of nucleotides, which store and copy genetic information. Cells build polymers by condensation and break them by hydrolysis.

sections.heading: Cell types
sections.text: Prokaryotic cells, bacteria and archaea, have no membrane-bound nucleus or organelles; their DNA is usually a single circular chromosome, and they have ribosomes. Eukaryotic cells, in animals, plants, fungi and protists, have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Mitochondria release energy as ATP; ribosomes make proteins; the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus process and transport proteins; lysosomes digest material; chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis in plants and algae. Case: a class compares a pond bacterium with onion epidermis cells. Both have a plasma membrane and ribosomes, but only the onion cells have a nucleus and mitochondria.

sections.heading: Membranes and transport
sections.text: The plasma membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins. It is selectively permeable. Diffusion moves particles from high to low concentration without energy. Osmosis is the diffusion of water across a semipermeable membrane from higher to lower water potential. Facilitated diffusion uses channel or carrier proteins. Active transport uses ATP to move substances against a concentration gradient. Endocytosis takes material in by vesicles; exocytosis releases it.

sections.heading: Enzymes and signals
sections.text: Enzymes are proteins that catalyse reactions by lowering activation energy. The substrate binds the active site; the enzyme is not used up. Heat or wrong pH can denature an enzyme by changing its shape. Cells communicate when a signal molecule, such as a hormone or neurotransmitter, binds a receptor. The receptor passes the message inside the cell, often by signal transduction, so the cell can respond.

keyPoints: Water is polar, has high specific heat and cohesion, and is the main solvent in cells.
Carbohydrates store energy and give structure; lipids store energy, form membranes and act as signals.
Proteins are amino acid chains that fold to perform enzyme, structural and transport roles.
Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus; eukaryotic cells have a nucleus and organelles.
The plasma membrane is selectively permeable; diffusion and osmosis are passive, while active transport uses ATP.
Enzymes lower activation energy and are denatured by heat or extreme pH; cell signals act through receptors.

en.title: Cell division, inheritance and molecular genetics
en.short: Mitosis, meiosis, chromosomes, DNA replication, gene expression, Mendelian and non-Mendelian inheritance, mutation.

sections.heading: Mitosis and meiosis
sections.text: Mitosis is nuclear division that produces two daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent cell. It supports growth and repair. Meiosis occurs in germ cells and has two divisions. It produces four haploid cells (gametes), each with half the chromosome number. Crossing over in prophase I and independent assortment in metaphase I create genetic variation. In animals, meiosis makes sperm and eggs; fertilisation restores the diploid number. A diploid cell with 2n = 8 gives gametes with n = 4 after meiosis.

sections.heading: Chromosomes and DNA
sections.text: Chromosomes are DNA wound around histone proteins. Most animal cells are diploid: chromosomes occur in homologous pairs, one from each parent. A gene is a DNA segment coding for a product; alleles are alternative forms. DNA replication is semi-conservative. Helicase unwinds the double helix, and DNA polymerase adds complementary bases (A with T, C with G) in the 5′ to 3′ direction. Each new molecule keeps one old strand. Uncorrected errors in copying are mutations.

sections.heading: Mendelian inheritance
sections.text: Mendel’s law of segregation says the two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation. His law of independent assortment says genes on different chromosomes assort independently. In a monohybrid cross Tt × Tt, a Punnett square gives TT, Tt, Tt, tt: 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, or 3 tall : 1 short. Non-Mendelian patterns include incomplete dominance (blended phenotype), codominance (both alleles expressed), multiple alleles, sex-linked genes and polygenic traits.

sections.heading: Expression and mutation
sections.text: Transcription copies a DNA gene into messenger RNA using RNA polymerase. In eukaryotes this happens in the nucleus. Translation uses ribosomes and transfer RNA to read mRNA codons and join amino acids into a protein. A mutation is a change in DNA sequence. A substitution may change one codon; an insertion or deletion can shift the reading frame. Germline mutations can be inherited; somatic mutations affect only the individual.

keyPoints: Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells; meiosis produces four haploid gametes and creates variation.
DNA replication is semi-conservative and uses complementary base pairing (A with T, C with G).
Monohybrid Tt × Tt gives a 3:1 phenotype ratio and a 1:2:1 genotype ratio.
Non-Mendelian inheritance includes incomplete dominance, codominance, multiple alleles, sex linkage and polygenic traits.
Transcription makes mRNA from DNA; translation joins amino acids into protein at ribosomes.
A frameshift mutation from an insertion or deletion changes the reading frame.

en.title: Evolution and natural selection
en.short: Evidence for evolution, Darwin and Wallace, mechanisms, adaptation, speciation and phylogenetic trees.

sections.heading: Evidence for evolution
sections.text:
Evolution is the change in inherited characteristics of a population over generations. Evidence comes from fossils (transitional forms), comparative anatomy (homologous structures with different functions), embryology, biogeography (island species resemble nearby mainland forms) and molecular similarities (DNA and proteins).

Darwin and Wallace independently proposed natural selection as the main mechanism. They argued that species are related by descent with modification.

sections.heading: Mechanisms of change
sections.text:
Four mechanisms change the frequencies of gene variants (alleles): mutation (creates new variants), gene flow (migration between populations), genetic drift (random change, stronger in small populations) and natural selection. Natural selection needs heritable variation, competition for limited resources, and differential survival and reproduction.

Individuals with traits better suited to the environment leave more offspring, so those traits become more common. This is adaptation. Example: in West Africa, the sickle cell trait (one HbS allele) gives some protection against malaria, so it persists at higher frequency than in non-malarial regions.

sections.heading: Adaptation and speciation
sections.text:
An adaptation is a trait that increases fitness (survival and reproduction) in a particular environment. Speciation is the splitting of one species into two. It usually begins when gene flow between populations is interrupted.

Allopatric speciation: a physical barrier (river, mountain) separates populations, which then diverge by mutation, drift and selection. Sympatric speciation: isolation without a barrier, for example polyploidy in plants or host shifts in insects. Over time, isolated populations become unable to interbreed.

sections.heading: Phylogenetic trees
sections.text:
Phylogenetic trees show evolutionary relationships. Each node is a common ancestor; branches are lineages. The root is the ancestor of all taxa in the tree.

Trees are built from shared derived characters (homologies) and molecular sequences. They are hypotheses that can be revised with new data. Relatedness is read from the most recent common ancestor, not from how far apart tips are drawn.

keyPoints: Evolution is change in inherited characteristics of a population over generations, supported by fossils, anatomy, biogeography and molecular evidence.
Darwin and Wallace proposed natural selection as the main mechanism of evolution.
Mechanisms of change are mutation, gene flow, genetic drift and natural selection.
Natural selection requires heritable variation and differential reproduction, leading to adaptation.
Speciation occurs when populations become reproductively isolated, often by geographic barriers (allopatric) or without them (sympatric).
Phylogenetic trees are hypotheses of evolutionary relationships based on shared derived characters and molecular data.

en.title: Animal classification and taxonomy
en.short: Naming, ranking and identifying animals, species concepts, reading trees and the major phyla.

sections.heading: Naming and ranking
sections.text:
Each species has a two-part scientific name: the genus (capitalised) and the specific epithet (lower case), both italicised in print and underlined in handwriting. The African bush elephant is Loxodonta africana. Animal names are governed by the International Code of Zoological Nomenclature (ICZN); plants and bacteria have separate codes. A name is tied to a type specimen kept in a collection, and the rule of priority means the earliest valid name is used.

Ranks run kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. Animalia is the kingdom. The Code does govern genus and family names; ranks above the family group, such as order, class and phylum, are conventions rather than Code rules, and authorities recognise roughly 30 to 35 animal phyla, the exact number varying.

sections.heading: Species concepts
sections.text: A species is the basic unit, but defining it is disputed. The biological species concept treats a species as populations that interbreed and are reproductively isolated from others; it fails for asexual organisms, fossils and many hybrids. The morphological concept uses consistent physical differences and suits fossils, but may split one variable species into several. The phylogenetic concept calls a species the smallest diagnosable group sharing an ancestor. Choose the concept to fit the organism and the question.

sections.heading: Keys and trees
sections.text:
A dichotomous key identifies a specimen by paired choices called couplets, each with two leads. Use clear, observable characters.

1a Jointed legs, exoskeleton: Arthropoda
1b No jointed legs: go to 2
2a Soft body, muscular foot: Mollusca
2b Spiny skin, tube feet: Echinodermata

A phylogenetic tree shows ancestry: tips are present-day taxa, nodes are ancestors, the root is oldest. Relatedness depends on how recently two taxa share an ancestor, not on how close they sit on the page. A clade is an ancestor with all its descendants. Shared ancestry gives homology; convergent evolution gives analogy, which misleads.

sections.heading: Major phyla
sections.text: The phyla usually taught are Porifera (sponges), Cnidaria, Platyhelminthes, Nematoda, Annelida, Mollusca, Arthropoda, Echinodermata and Chordata. They differ in symmetry, body cavity, segmentation and development. Arthropoda is the largest phylum.

keyPoints: A binomial name is genus plus specific epithet, italicised, with the genus capitalised.
Ranks are kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
Biological, morphological and phylogenetic species concepts each suit different organisms.
A dichotomous key uses paired leads with clear, observable characters.
On a tree, relatedness means recency of common ancestry, not position on the page.
A clade is an ancestor plus all its descendants; homology reflects shared ancestry, analogy does not.

en.title: Invertebrate diversity: body plans and life strategies
en.short: Body plans, symmetry, segmentation, feeding and reproduction across the main invertebrate phyla.

sections.heading: Body plans
sections.text: Invertebrates are animals without a backbone. A body plan is the basic arrangement of tissues, symmetry and body cavity. Sponges (Porifera) have no true tissues and are asymmetrical. Cnidarians (jellyfish, corals) have radial symmetry and a sac body plan with one opening. Most other phyla are bilaterally symmetrical, often with a head end. Many have a coelom, a fluid-filled body cavity lined by mesoderm. Roundworms (Nematoda) are unsegmented and have a pseudocoelom, a cavity not fully lined by mesoderm. Segmentation, the division of the body into repeated units, is clear in annelids (earthworms) and arthropods (insects, crabs). Echinoderm adults show radial symmetry, but their larvae are bilateral.

sections.heading: Feeding and roles
sections.text: Feeding strategies follow body plans. Sponges and bivalve molluscs filter particles from water. Cnidarians use stinging cells to catch plankton. Molluscs often scrape food with a radula; cephalopods such as octopus use a beak. Arthropods have jointed appendages and mouthparts for biting, sucking or chewing. Echinoderms use tube feet. These animals shape ecosystems: corals build reefs, earthworms aerate soil, and insects pollinate crops. Case: in a Nigerian mangrove creek, Chidi finds filter-feeding oysters clearing water and burrowing polychaete worms reworking the mud.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Reproduction is varied. Sponges and cnidarians can reproduce asexually by budding or fragmentation. Many marine invertebrates release eggs and sperm into water, so fertilisation is external. Arthropods and cephalopods usually fertilise internally. Earthworms are hermaphrodites, each worm having both male and female organs, but they cross-fertilise. Parasitic flatworms (Platyhelminthes) often have complex life cycles with more than one host. A larva is an immature stage that differs from the adult. Examples include the trochophore of molluscs and annelids and the nauplius of crustaceans. Such life cycles connect marine, freshwater and land food webs.

keyPoints: Invertebrates lack a backbone and show a wide range of body plans.
Sponges have no true tissues; cnidarians have radial symmetry and a single body opening.
Bilateral symmetry and a head end are linked with active movement in many phyla.
Segmentation repeats body units and is well seen in annelids and arthropods.
Feeding modes include filter feeding, stinging, radula scraping and jointed mouthparts.
Reproduction ranges from asexual budding to sexual external or internal fertilisation, often with larval stages.

en.title: Vertebrate diversity: fishes to mammals
en.short: Classification, adaptations and examples of fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.

sections.heading: What is a vertebrate?
sections.text: Vertebrates are animals with a vertebral column (backbone) and a skull. In classification they form the subphylum Vertebrata within the phylum Chordata. Traditional courses divide living vertebrates into jawless fishes, cartilaginous fishes, bony fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. These groups are convenient grades rather than a perfect evolutionary tree: fishes are not one natural class, and modern schemes often place birds inside Reptilia. Check your syllabus for the scheme it uses.

sections.heading: Fishes and amphibians
sections.text:
Fishes live mainly in water. They use gills to take oxygen from water, fins and a streamlined body to swim, and a lateral line to sense water movement. Most are ectothermic, meaning body temperature follows the surroundings. Examples are Nile tilapia (a bony fish) and sharks (cartilaginous fishes).

Amphibians have moist, permeable skin that also exchanges gases. Most lay eggs in water, and the larvae, such as tadpoles, metamorphose into adults. They are ectothermic. The African clawed frog is a common example.

sections.heading: Reptiles and birds
sections.text:
Reptiles have dry skin covered with keratinised scales, breathe with lungs, and usually lay an amniotic egg. This egg has membranes that protect the embryo and reduce dependence on water. Most reptiles are ectothermic. Examples are the Nile crocodile and African rock python.

Birds have feathers, wings, a beak and a high metabolism. They are endothermic, meaning they generate heat internally, and lay amniotic eggs. The cattle egret is a familiar African bird.

sections.heading: Mammals and case
sections.text:
Mammals have hair or fur and mammary glands that produce milk. They are endothermic, and most give birth to live young; monotremes are the egg-laying exception. A diaphragm helps ventilation, and three middle ear bones improve hearing. The African elephant is an example.

Case: compare a Nile crocodile with a cattle egret. Both lay amniotic eggs, but the crocodile is ectothermic and scaly, while the egret is endothermic and feathered. Such comparisons show how structure fits habitat.

keyPoints: Vertebrates have a vertebral column and skull and belong to the subphylum Vertebrata.

Traditional classes are jawless fishes, cartilaginous fishes, bony fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals, but fishes are not a natural group, and reptiles are not a natural group unless birds are included in Reptilia.
Fishes use gills, fins and a lateral line; amphibians have moist skin and usually metamorphose from aquatic larvae.
Reptiles and birds lay amniotic eggs; reptiles are mostly ectothermic, while birds are endothermic and feathered.
Mammals have hair and mammary glands, are endothermic, and most bear live young.
Ectothermic animals rely on surroundings for heat; endothermic animals generate heat internally.

en.title: Animal form and function: tissues and homeostasis
en.short: Four tissue types, organ systems, and how feedback keeps temperature and water balance steady.

sections.heading: Four tissues
sections.text:
Animal bodies are built from four tissue types. Epithelial tissue covers surfaces and lines cavities; its cells sit close together, and it may be simple (one layer) or stratified (several layers). Connective tissue supports and binds other tissues; it has cells scattered in an extracellular matrix, which may be fibrous, gel-like or hard (as in bone).

Muscle tissue contracts: skeletal muscle moves the body, smooth muscle moves internal organs, and cardiac muscle pumps blood in the heart. Nervous tissue conducts electrical impulses; it contains neurons and supporting glial cells. An organ is two or more tissues working together, such as the stomach.

sections.heading: Organ systems
sections.text:
Organ systems are groups of organs with a shared function. Examples include the digestive, respiratory, circulatory, excretory, nervous, endocrine, immune, skeletal and reproductive systems.

They are not independent: the circulatory system carries substances that the digestive and respiratory systems take in, while nerves and hormones coordinate their activity. This coordination is the basis of homeostasis.

sections.heading: Feedback control
sections.text:
Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment around a set point (target value), despite changes outside. It usually works by negative feedback: a sensor detects a change, a control centre compares it with the set point, and an effector produces a response that opposes the change.

For example, if body temperature rises, blood vessels in the skin widen and sweating increases, so heat is lost. Positive feedback amplifies a change and is less common; it helps complete processes such as childbirth.

sections.heading: Temperature and water
sections.text:
Temperature balance depends on heat gained from metabolism and the environment and heat lost by radiation, conduction, convection and evaporation. Water balance depends on intake and loss through urine, faeces, sweat and breath.

In a hot dry place, a person may lose much water by sweating; if water is not replaced, blood plasma becomes more concentrated. Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) release increases, and the kidneys reabsorb more water, producing less urine. This is negative feedback. The exact responses vary among animals and habitats.

keyPoints: Epithelial tissue covers and lines surfaces; connective tissue supports and binds; muscle tissue contracts; nervous tissue conducts impulses.
An organ is two or more tissues working together, and an organ system is a group of organs with a shared function.
Homeostasis keeps the internal environment near a set point by negative feedback.
A negative feedback loop has a sensor, a control centre and an effector that opposes the change.
Temperature balance is heat gain versus heat loss; water balance is intake versus loss.
When water loss is high, antidiuretic hormone (ADH) reduces urine volume, but responses vary between animals and habitats.

en.title: Introduction to ecology and biomes
en.short: Organism-environment links, abiotic factors, energy flow, nutrient cycles, biomes and basic ecological levels.

sections.heading: Ecology and abiotic factors
sections.text: Ecology is the study of how organisms interact with each other and with their environment. The environment has abiotic (non-living) parts such as temperature, water, light, salinity, pH and soil, and biotic (living) parts such as food and predators. Each species survives within a range of tolerance for each factor; outside that range the factor limits its distribution. A limiting factor is the one in shortest supply. For example, water limits plant growth in a savanna dry season.

sections.heading: Energy flow and nutrient cycles
sections.text: An ecosystem is a community of organisms plus its abiotic surroundings. Energy enters mainly as sunlight, is captured by producers (plants, algae) and passes through trophic levels: primary consumers, secondary consumers and so on. Decomposers break down dead material from every level. Energy is lost as heat at each step, so food chains are short. A rough illustration: if producers store 20,000 kJ, about 2,000 kJ may reach primary consumers and 200 kJ secondary consumers at 10% transfer; real efficiency varies, often 5 to 20%. Unlike energy, nutrients such as carbon, nitrogen and water cycle between organisms and the environment.

sections.heading: Biomes
sections.text: A biome is a large region with a characteristic climate and community, especially plants. Temperature and rainfall decide the main terrestrial biomes: tropical rainforest, savanna, desert, temperate grassland, temperate forest, taiga (boreal forest) and tundra. Each has typical adaptations, such as drought-tolerant plants in deserts and cold-tolerant conifers in taiga. Aquatic biomes (freshwater and marine) are classified by salinity, depth and flow.

sections.heading: Populations and communities
sections.text: A population is a group of one species in one area. Its size changes through births, deaths, immigration and emigration; carrying capacity is the maximum the environment can support. A community is all populations living together. Species interact through competition, predation and symbiosis. These ideas are developed later in population and community ecology.

keyPoints: Ecology studies organism-environment interactions; abiotic factors include temperature, water, light and soil.
Energy flows one way through trophic levels and is lost as heat; nutrients cycle.
A biome is a large region shaped by climate, such as savanna, desert or taiga.
A population is one species in an area; a community is all populations; an ecosystem adds the abiotic environment.
Limiting factors and tolerance ranges control where species can live.
Rough 10% transfer between trophic levels is only an illustration; real efficiency varies.

en.title: Comparative animal anatomy and histology
en.short: Comparative organ anatomy and how histological sections are prepared, read and linked to function.

sections.heading: Comparative organ anatomy
sections.text:
Comparative anatomy asks how the same organ is built in different animals. Homologous organs share an evolutionary origin even when they look different, such as the vertebrate forelimb. Analogous organs do the same job without shared origin, such as the fish gill and the insect trachea.

In the heart, a bony fish has one atrium and one ventricle in series, so blood passes once per circuit. Amphibians have two atria and one ventricle. Mammals and birds have four chambers. Invertebrates may have open systems, where haemolymph bathes organs, or closed systems with vessels.

sections.heading: Preparing sections
sections.text:
Histology is the study of tissue structure in thin sections. Preparation follows fixed steps: fixation in formalin, dehydration through alcohols, clearing in a solvent such as xylene, embedding in paraffin wax, sectioning on a microtome, and staining.

Paraffin sections are commonly about 4 to 10 micrometres thick. In haematoxylin and eosin (H&E), haematoxylin, a basic dye, colours acidic nuclei blue to purple; eosin, an acidic dye, colours cytoplasm and collagen pink. Frozen sections cut on a cryostat give rapid answers. Artefacts such as folds, tears and shrinkage must not be mistaken for real structure.

sections.heading: Reading a section
sections.text:
Reading a section means identifying tissue type, organ and orientation. Epithelia are sheets of cells on a basement membrane, named by cell shape and layer number. Connective tissue is recognised by its extracellular matrix.

Plane of section matters. A tubule cut transversely looks like a ring; cut obliquely it looks like an ellipse. Scale is checked with a stage micrometer. If a structure measures 40 mm on a print at ×400, its real size is 40 mm ÷ 400 = 0.1 mm, or 100 micrometres.

sections.heading: Structure to function
sections.text: Structure supports function. Thin alveolar walls and a large surface area aid gas exchange. Fish gills use countercurrent flow, and intestinal villi increase absorption area. In each case the shape of the tissue explains the job it does.

keyPoints: Homologous organs share an origin; analogous organs share a function.
Paraffin histology runs fixation, dehydration, clearing, embedding, sectioning and staining.
In H&E, haematoxylin stains nuclei blue to purple and eosin stains cytoplasm pink.
Section plane changes apparent shape: a tubule cut across looks like a ring, obliquely like an ellipse.
Real size = measured size on the image ÷ magnification.
Tissue structure predicts function, as in thin alveolar walls or countercurrent fish gills.

en.title: Comparative animal physiology: respiration, circulation and excretion
en.short: Gas exchange, circulatory systems, blood, osmoregulation, excretion and acid-base balance across animals.

sections.heading: Gas exchange
sections.text: Gas exchange is diffusion of O2 and CO2 across a thin, moist, permeable surface. Its rate depends on surface area, concentration gradient and diffusion distance, as Fick’s law states: rate ∝ area × gradient ÷ thickness. Water breathers use gills; many fish use countercurrent flow, where water and blood move in opposite directions, keeping a gradient along the gill. Air breathers use lungs, tracheae or skin. Ventilation and perfusion must match: a fish with cardiac output 200 mL/min and an arteriovenous O2 difference of 8 mL per 100 mL takes up 200 × 0.08 = 16 mL O2/min.

sections.heading: Circulation and blood
sections.text: Circulatory systems move respiratory gases, nutrients, wastes and heat. Open systems, as in most arthropods and many molluscs, pump haemolymph into sinuses. Closed systems, as in annelids, cephalopods and vertebrates, keep blood in vessels, allowing higher pressure and flow control. Hearts may be tubular, chambered or multiple. Blood carries respiratory pigments: haemoglobin (iron), haemocyanin (copper) and chlorocruorin. Pigments raise oxygen capacity and show the Bohr effect: lower pH or higher CO2 reduces oxygen affinity and aids unloading.

sections.heading: Osmoregulation and excretion
sections.text: Osmoregulation controls water and solute balance. Osmoconformers match body fluid to the environment; osmoregulators keep it different, using energy. Freshwater animals gain water and lose salts, so they excrete dilute urine and take up salts. Marine teleosts lose water and gain salts, so they drink seawater and excrete concentrated salts via gills or kidneys. Nitrogenous waste is ammonia (toxic, water-soluble), urea (less toxic) or uric acid (semi-solid, saves water). Excretory organs include nephridia, Malpighian tubules, antennal glands and kidneys; they filter or secrete, then reabsorb useful materials.

sections.heading: Acid-base balance
sections.text: Acid-base balance keeps body fluid pH stable, near 7.4 in vertebrates but variable. Buffers such as bicarbonate and proteins resist pH change. Ventilation removes CO2, and excretion removes H+ or HCO3−. Kidneys or equivalents adjust bicarbonate reabsorption. In fish, gill ion exchange is important. These systems interact: ventilation alters CO2 and pH, and pH alters oxygen binding.

keyPoints: Gas exchange rate follows Fick’s law: rate ∝ area × gradient ÷ thickness.
Oxygen uptake can be estimated as cardiac output × arteriovenous O2 difference.
Countercurrent flow in fish gills keeps a diffusion gradient along the gill.
Open circulatory systems pump haemolymph into sinuses; closed systems keep blood in vessels.
Osmoregulators use energy to keep body fluids different from the environment; osmoconformers do not.
Nitrogenous waste is excreted as ammonia, urea or uric acid, and acid-base balance uses buffers, ventilation and ion excretion.

en.title: Nutrition, digestion and energy metabolism
en.short: Feeding strategies, guts and enzymes, absorption, metabolic rate, energy budgets and thermoregulation.

sections.heading: Feeding and guts
sections.text:
Animals use feeding strategies such as filter feeding, deposit feeding, herbivory, carnivory and fluid feeding. A gastrovascular cavity has one opening; most animals have a complete alimentary canal with mouth and anus, allowing regional specialisation.

Regions may include a grinding mouth, storage stomach, enzyme-secreting intestine and a caecum or rumen where microbes ferment plant fibre. Ruminants ferment in the foregut (rumen) before the true stomach; horses and rabbits ferment in the hindgut. Herbivores usually need longer retention times than carnivores.

sections.heading: Enzymes and absorption
sections.text:
Digestion is the breakdown of food, chemically by enzymes and mechanically by grinding and churning. Amylase hydrolyses starch; proteases such as pepsin and trypsin break proteins into peptides and amino acids; lipases split fats into fatty acids and glycerol. Each enzyme works best at a particular pH: pepsin is acid, trypsin alkaline.

Absorption occurs mainly in the small intestine, where villi and microvilli increase surface area. Nutrients cross by diffusion, facilitated diffusion or active transport. Water and ions are reclaimed in the large intestine. Undigested material is egested as faeces.

sections.heading: Metabolic rate
sections.text:
Metabolic rate is the rate at which an animal uses energy, often measured as oxygen consumption. Basal metabolic rate (BMR) is measured in a resting, post-absorptive endotherm at a thermoneutral temperature; standard metabolic rate (SMR) is the equivalent for an ectotherm at a stated temperature.

Mass-specific metabolic rate is higher in small animals because they have a larger surface area relative to volume. Q10 is the factor by which rate rises for a 10 °C increase, commonly about 2 to 3.

sections.heading: Energy budgets and heat
sections.text:
An energy budget tracks energy flow: ingestion (I) = egestion (E) + assimilation (A), and A = respiration (R) + production (P) + excretion (U). Production is growth and reproduction. Example: I = 500 kJ/day, E = 150, U = 50, R = 200, so P = 500 − 150 − 50 − 200 = 100 kJ/day.

Thermoregulation is control of body temperature. Endotherms use metabolic heat; ectotherms rely mainly on external heat. Insulation, evaporative cooling, shivering and behaviour help balance heat gain and loss.

keyPoints: Feeding strategies include filter, deposit, herbivory, carnivory and fluid feeding; gut structure reflects diet.
Digestion uses amylase, proteases and lipases, each with a preferred pH; absorption occurs mainly in the small intestine.
Metabolic rate is energy use per unit time; BMR applies to endotherms and SMR to ectotherms under stated conditions.
Mass-specific metabolic rate is higher in small animals; Q10 describes the rise in rate for a 10 °C increase.
Energy budget: I = E + A and A = R + P + U, so production P = I − E − R − U.
Endotherms use metabolic heat and ectotherms rely mainly on external heat; both balance heat gain and loss.

en.title: Endocrine and reproductive biology
en.short: Hormone action, feedback, endocrine glands, gametogenesis, cycles, fertilisation and reproductive strategies.

sections.heading: Hormone action
sections.text:
A hormone is a chemical signal released into the blood and carried to target cells that have receptors. Peptide hormones usually bind receptors on the cell surface and act through second messengers. Steroid hormones enter cells and bind intracellular receptors, often changing gene transcription.

Feedback keeps most endocrine systems stable. Negative feedback reverses a change. Case: after a meal, blood glucose rises. Pancreatic beta cells release insulin, which helps cells take up glucose and store it as glycogen. As glucose falls, insulin secretion falls. Positive feedback amplifies a change; oxytocin during birth is an example.

sections.heading: Endocrine glands
sections.text:
Endocrine glands are ductless glands that secrete hormones. Major examples are the hypothalamus, pituitary, thyroid, adrenal glands, pancreas and gonads. The hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems.

In reproduction, the hypothalamus releases GnRH. The anterior pituitary releases FSH and LH. The gonads release sex steroids such as oestrogen and testosterone. This chain is the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Sex steroids usually exert negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, but a mid-cycle LH surge in females is driven by positive feedback.

sections.heading: Gametes and cycles
sections.text:
Gametogenesis is the production of haploid gametes by meiosis and maturation. Spermatogenesis gives four sperm from one primary spermatocyte. Oogenesis gives one ovum and polar bodies, because cytoplasm is divided unequally.

Reproductive cycles prepare the body for fertilisation. Many non-primate mammals have an oestrous cycle, with sexual receptivity limited to oestrus. Many primates, including humans, have a menstrual cycle, with endometrial shedding. Both involve follicle growth, ovulation and a corpus luteum. Day length can entrain cycles.

sections.heading: Fertilisation and strategies
sections.text:
Fertilisation is the fusion of sperm and egg nuclei. The sperm acrosome reaction releases enzymes, and membrane fusion triggers a block to polyspermy, preventing extra sperm from entering.

Reproductive strategies differ. Broadcast spawning with external fertilisation releases many gametes into water and gives little parental care. Internal fertilisation, oviparity (laying eggs), viviparity (young developing inside the mother) and parental care usually mean fewer gametes but higher survival.

keyPoints: Hormones are chemical signals carried in blood to target cells with receptors; peptide hormones act at the surface, steroid hormones inside cells.
Negative feedback reverses change and stabilises hormone levels; positive feedback amplifies change, as in the oxytocin surge during birth.
The hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis links GnRH, FSH and LH to sex steroid release, usually under negative feedback.
Gametogenesis uses meiosis: spermatogenesis gives four sperm, while oogenesis gives one ovum and polar bodies.
Oestrous cycles occur in many non-primate mammals and menstrual cycles in many primates; both include ovulation and a corpus luteum.
Fertilisation involves the acrosome reaction and a block to polyspermy; reproductive strategies range from broadcast spawning to viviparity and parental care.

en.title: Developmental biology and embryology
en.short: Fertilisation, cleavage, gastrulation, organogenesis, metamorphosis, regeneration and developmental genes.

sections.heading: Fertilisation and cleavage
sections.text:
Fertilisation is the fusion of a sperm and an egg. In animals, the sperm undergoes the acrosome reaction, releasing enzymes that help it reach the egg membrane. The egg then undergoes the cortical reaction, which changes the coat and blocks polyspermy, the entry of more than one sperm.

Fusion restores the diploid chromosome number and activates development. Cleavage follows: rapid mitotic divisions without growth, producing smaller cells called blastomeres. These form a hollow ball, the blastula, with a fluid-filled cavity, the blastocoel.

sections.heading: Gastrulation and organogenesis
sections.text:
Gastrulation rearranges the blastula into three germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. Cells move by invagination, involution and migration, forming the archenteron, the primitive gut, and the blastopore, its opening. The germ layers later give skin and nervous system, muscle and skeleton, and gut lining.

Organogenesis builds organs. In vertebrates, the dorsal ectoderm thickens into the neural plate, which folds into the neural tube. Mesoderm forms somites, blocks that become vertebrae and muscles. Induction, where one tissue signals another, is central; the amphibian organiser is a classic example.

sections.heading: Metamorphosis and regeneration
sections.text:
Metamorphosis is a post-embryonic change in body form. In amphibians, thyroid hormones drive tail resorption and limb growth. In insects, ecdysone and juvenile hormone control moulting and metamorphosis, such as the change from larva to pupa to adult.

Regeneration replaces lost parts. In epimorphosis, as in salamander limbs, a blastema of dividing cells grows a new structure. In morphallaxis, as in Hydra, existing tissue remodels. Planaria are famous for regeneration.

sections.heading: Genetic control
sections.text:
Development is controlled by differential gene expression. Maternal effect genes set up axes. Segmentation genes divide the Drosophila embryo. Hox genes specify body regions. Signalling pathways such as Wnt, BMP and Notch coordinate induction.

A concrete case: in Xenopus laevis, the African clawed frog used in teaching labs, sperm entry triggers cortical rotation; the opposite side becomes dorsal and forms the organiser.

keyPoints: Fertilisation restores diploidy and triggers the cortical reaction that blocks polyspermy.
Cleavage divides the zygote into blastomeres without growth, forming the blastula.
Gastrulation forms ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm and the archenteron.
Organogenesis depends on induction, as in neural tube formation.
Metamorphosis is controlled by hormones such as thyroid hormones in amphibians and ecdysone in insects.
Regeneration can occur by epimorphosis with a blastema or by morphallaxis, and Hox genes and signalling pathways control regional identity.

en.title: Neurobiology: neurons, sensory systems and motor control
en.short: Neuron signalling, synapses, sensory transduction, motor control and comparative nervous systems.

sections.heading: Neuron signalling
sections.text: A neuron has dendrites for input, a cell body, and an axon for output. At the axon hillock, graded inputs sum. If threshold is reached, voltage-gated Na+ channels open and an action potential fires. K+ efflux then repolarises the membrane and briefly hyperpolarises it. The refractory period limits firing rate and keeps signals one-way. Myelin speeds conduction by saltatory jumping between nodes of Ranvier. The Nernst equation gives one ion’s equilibrium potential: at 37 °C, E_K = 61.5 log10(5/140) = −89 mV for 5 mM K+ outside and 140 mM inside. Real resting potential is less negative because Na+ leaks in.

sections.heading: Synapses
sections.text: At a chemical synapse, an action potential depolarises the presynaptic terminal, Ca2+ enters, and neurotransmitter vesicles fuse. Transmitter binds postsynaptic receptors and opens ion channels, producing an excitatory or inhibitory postsynaptic potential (EPSP or IPSP). These graded potentials sum in space and time; if threshold is reached, the postsynaptic neuron fires. Electrical synapses use gap junctions and are faster but less modifiable. Chemical synapses allow amplification, inhibition and plasticity.

sections.heading: Senses and motor control
sections.text: Sensory receptors transduce stimuli into receptor potentials. They encode modality, location, intensity (firing rate) and duration (adaptation). Motor neurons activate muscles. A motor unit is one motor neuron and the muscle fibres it innervates. Reflex arcs connect sensory input to rapid output without conscious control. Higher centres refine posture, locomotion and learned movement. In many animals, sensory and motor pathways cross the midline, but the details vary.

sections.heading: Comparative organisation
sections.text: Nervous systems range from nerve nets in cnidarians to segmented nerve cords in annelids and arthropods, and centralised brains in cephalopods and vertebrates. Cephalisation concentrates sensory and integrative neurons at the front end. Vertebrate brains show regional specialisation: hindbrain for basic functions, midbrain for sensory processing, forebrain for integration and learning. These are general patterns; details vary across taxa.

keyPoints: Action potentials are all-or-none, start at the axon hillock when threshold is reached, and travel faster when myelinated by saltatory conduction.
The Nernst equation at 37 °C for a monovalent cation is E = 61.5 log10([out]/[in]) mV.
Chemical synapses release neurotransmitter, producing EPSPs or IPSPs that sum in space and time.
Sensory receptors transduce stimuli and encode intensity mainly by firing rate.
A motor unit is one motor neuron and the muscle fibres it innervates.
Nervous systems range from nerve nets to centralised brains with cephalisation, but patterns vary across taxa.

en.title: Immunology: innate and adaptive immunity
en.short: Barriers, phagocytosis, inflammation, lymphocytes, antibodies, MHC, immune memory, vaccines and comparative immunity.

sections.heading: Innate barriers
sections.text:
Innate immunity is the fast, non-specific first defence. Barriers include skin, mucus and cilia in airways, stomach acid and lysozyme in tears.

If a microbe crosses a barrier, phagocytes such as neutrophils and macrophages engulf it by phagocytosis. Complement proteins and natural killer cells also attack microbes or infected cells. Innate receptors, such as Toll-like receptors, recognise common microbial patterns. This response is immediate but has no memory.

sections.heading: Inflammation and phagocytosis
sections.text:
Inflammation is the local response to injury or infection: redness, heat, swelling and pain. Chemical signals widen blood vessels and attract phagocytes. Neutrophils arrive first, then macrophages.

Phagocytosis has steps: recognition, engulfment into a phagosome, fusion with a lysosome, and killing by enzymes and reactive oxygen. Case: Ada steps on a thorn. The site becomes red and swollen; neutrophils phagocytose bacteria.

sections.heading: Adaptive immunity
sections.text:
Adaptive immunity is slower, specific and remembered. Lymphocytes are white blood cells. B lymphocytes mature in bone marrow (in birds, in the bursa of Fabricius) and can become plasma cells that secrete antibodies.

Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins with variable regions that bind a specific antigen (any molecule the immune system recognises). T lymphocytes mature in the thymus. Helper T cells (CD4+) coordinate the response; cytotoxic T cells (CD8+) kill infected cells. Clonal selection expands only the lymphocytes whose receptors fit the antigen.

sections.heading: MHC, memory and vaccines
sections.text:
The major histocompatibility complex (MHC) is a set of cell-surface proteins that display peptide fragments to T cells. MHC class I is on nearly all nucleated cells and presents to CD8+ cells; MHC class II is on antigen-presenting cells and presents to CD4+ cells. In humans the MHC is called HLA.

After infection, memory B and T cells remain, so a second exposure gives a faster, stronger response. Vaccines safely expose the immune system to antigens to create this memory. Comparative immunity varies: invertebrates rely mainly on innate defences, while jawed vertebrates have MHC-based adaptive immunity.

keyPoints: Innate immunity is fast, non-specific and has no memory; barriers, phagocytes and inflammation are its main parts.
Phagocytosis proceeds by recognition, engulfment into a phagosome, lysosome fusion and killing.
Adaptive immunity is specific and remembered: B cells secrete antibodies and T cells help or kill.
MHC class I presents to CD8+ T cells, while MHC class II presents to CD4+ T cells.
Memory B and T cells make a second response faster and stronger, and vaccines create this memory safely.
Invertebrates rely mainly on innate immunity, while jawed vertebrates have MHC-based adaptive immunity.

en.title: Parasitology and disease vectors
en.short: Protozoan, helminth and arthropod parasites, their life cycles, transmission and control.

sections.heading: Parasite groups
sections.text: Parasitism is a relationship in which one organism, the parasite, lives on or in another, the host, and gains nutrients at the host’s expense. Protozoa are single-celled parasites such as Plasmodium, the cause of malaria. Helminths are parasitic worms, including flukes, tapeworms and roundworms. Arthropods may be parasites themselves, such as lice and ticks, or disease vectors that carry pathogens between hosts. A vector is an organism, often an insect, that transmits an infectious agent.

sections.heading: Life cycles and hosts
sections.text: Parasites often have complex life cycles with more than one host. The definitive host is where the parasite reaches sexual maturity; the intermediate host is where larval or asexual stages develop. In malaria, female Anopheles mosquitoes are definitive hosts because Plasmodium sexual stages form in them, while humans are intermediate hosts. In schistosomiasis, humans are definitive hosts and freshwater snails are intermediate hosts. Schistosoma eggs reach water, hatch, infect snails, and release cercariae, free-swimming larvae, that penetrate human skin. Knowing each stage helps identify weak points for control.

sections.heading: Transmission and interactions
sections.text: Transmission may be direct, through food, water, soil or skin contact, or indirect, through vectors or intermediate hosts. Host-parasite interactions involve immune attack, immune evasion and coevolution. A parasite that kills its host too quickly may reduce its own spread, so virulence is often balanced against transmission. Some infections are zoonoses, meaning they pass from animals to humans. Diagnosis uses microscopy, serology or molecular tests, chosen for the parasite and setting.

sections.heading: Control and example
sections.text: Control combines treatment, vector control, safe water and sanitation, and health education. Insecticide-treated nets and indoor spraying reduce malaria transmission, but insecticide resistance must be monitored. Schistosomiasis control uses praziquantel, snail control and avoiding contaminated water. In a lakeside town, school children who swim in snail-infested water may be treated and taught to use safe water points; this cuts egg contamination and new infections. No single measure is enough; integrated control is usual.

keyPoints: Parasitism is a relationship in which a parasite gains nutrients at the host’s expense.
The definitive host is where the parasite reaches sexual maturity; the intermediate host is where larval or asexual stages develop.
In malaria, female Anopheles mosquitoes are definitive hosts and humans are intermediate hosts.
In schistosomiasis, humans are definitive hosts and freshwater snails are intermediate hosts.
A vector is an organism that transmits an infectious agent between hosts.
Control is integrated: treatment, vector control, water and sanitation, and health education, with resistance monitored.

en.title: Entomology: insect biology and economic importance
en.short: Covers insect body plan, metamorphosis, orders, ecology, pollination, pests and vector control.

sections.heading: Body plan
sections.text:
Insects are arthropods in the class Insecta. The adult body has three tagmata: head, thorax and abdomen. The head bears antennae, compound eyes and mouthparts; the thorax bears three pairs of legs and usually two pairs of wings; the abdomen holds the gut and reproductive organs.

A chitinous exoskeleton supports and protects the body and limits water loss, but it must be moulted for growth. Gas exchange uses tracheae, the circulatory system is open, and excretion uses Malpighian tubules.

sections.heading: Metamorphosis and orders
sections.text:
Metamorphosis is the change from immature to adult form. Ametabolous insects moult with little change. Hemimetabolous insects pass through egg, nymph and adult; the nymph resembles the adult but lacks wings and working reproductive organs. Holometabolous insects pass through egg, larva, pupa and adult; the larva feeds and the pupa reorganises the body.

Orders are classified by wings, mouthparts and metamorphosis. Common orders include Coleoptera (beetles), Lepidoptera (butterflies and moths), Hymenoptera (bees, wasps, ants), Diptera (flies), Hemiptera (true bugs) and Orthoptera (grasshoppers).

sections.heading: Ecology and benefits
sections.text:
Insects are central to ecology. Many are pollinators and carry pollen between flowers; many crops and wild plants depend on animal pollination. Others decompose dead matter and recycle nutrients.

People use honey and beeswax from honey bees, silk from Bombyx mori larvae, and biological control. In biological control, a natural enemy is introduced or conserved to reduce a pest. The cassava mealybug, a serious pest of cassava in Africa, was brought under control by the introduced parasitoid wasp Anagyrus lopezi.

sections.heading: Pests and vector control
sections.text:
Insect pests reduce yields by feeding on leaves, stems, fruit and stored grain, and some transmit plant viruses. Vectors transmit pathogens: Anopheles mosquitoes transmit malaria, Aedes mosquitoes transmit dengue and yellow fever, and tsetse flies transmit trypanosomiasis.

Integrated vector management combines methods: remove breeding sites, use larvicides or adulticides, use insecticide-treated nets and indoor residual spraying where approved, and rotate insecticides to limit resistance. Approved methods differ by country and disease, so check current WHO and national guidelines.

keyPoints: Insects are arthropods with three body regions, three pairs of legs and a chitinous exoskeleton.
Complete metamorphosis has egg, larva, pupa and adult; incomplete metamorphosis has egg, nymph and adult.
Main insect orders include Coleoptera, Lepidoptera, Hymenoptera, Diptera, Hemiptera and Orthoptera.
Insects pollinate plants, decompose organic matter and provide honey, silk and biological control.
Insect pests damage crops and stored products, and some insects transmit human and animal diseases.
Integrated vector management combines environmental, biological and chemical methods and manages insecticide resistance; follow national guidelines.

en.title: Animal behaviour and behavioural ecology: mechanism, function and evolution
en.short: Innate and learned behaviour, communication, foraging, mating, kin selection, social behaviour and methods.

sections.heading: Innate and learned
sections.text:
An innate behaviour develops without specific experience and is inherited, such as a fixed action pattern triggered by a sign stimulus. A learned behaviour changes with experience. Habituation is learning to stop responding to a repeated harmless stimulus.

Imprinting, studied by Konrad Lorenz, occurs during a sensitive period early in life. Classical conditioning pairs a neutral stimulus with a reward or punishment; operant conditioning shapes behaviour by its consequences. Most behaviour lies between these extremes, because genes and environment interact.

sections.heading: Communication and foraging
sections.text:
Communication is the transfer of information from a sender to a receiver. Signals may be visual, acoustic, chemical or tactile. Honest signals are reliable because costly to fake. Foraging theory treats feeding as a cost-benefit problem. Net energy gain rate = (energy gained − energy cost) ÷ time.

Example: patch A gives 60 kJ for 20 kJ cost in 30 min: (60 − 20) ÷ 30 = 1.33 kJ/min. Patch B gives 90 kJ for 50 kJ in 60 min: (90 − 50) ÷ 60 = 0.67 kJ/min. A is better.

sections.heading: Mating and kin
sections.text:
Mating systems are monogamy, polygyny, polyandry or promiscuity. Parental investment helps explain them: the sex that invests more tends to be choosier.

Kin selection, through inclusive fitness, explains altruism toward relatives. Hamilton’s rule says a helping gene spreads if rB > C, where r is relatedness, B is the benefit to the recipient and C is the cost to the helper. For full siblings r = 0.5. If helping adds 4 offspring and costs 1, rB = 0.5 × 4 = 2 > 1, so helping is favoured.

sections.heading: Social behaviour and methods
sections.text:
Group living brings benefits such as better predator detection and dilution of risk, but also costs such as competition and disease.

Behaviour is studied by observation, controlled experiments and the comparative method. Focal sampling follows one animal; scan sampling records all animals at intervals. Tinbergen proposed four questions: mechanism, development, function and evolution. Researchers must consider observer effects and animal welfare.

keyPoints: Innate behaviour develops without specific experience; learned behaviour changes with experience.
Communication transfers information from a sender to a receiver and is often mutually beneficial.
Optimal foraging compares net energy gain rate: (energy gained − energy cost) ÷ time.
Hamilton’s rule rB > C predicts when altruism toward relatives is favoured.
Mating systems are shaped by parental investment and sexual selection.
Behaviour is studied by observation, experiment and Tinbergen’s four questions.

en.title: Population and community ecology
en.short: Demography, life tables, population growth, species interactions, succession and biodiversity measurement.

sections.heading: Demography and life tables
sections.text:
Demography is the study of births, deaths and movement in a population. A life table follows a cohort, a group born at the same time, and records survivorship lx and fecundity mx at each age x. The net reproductive rate is R0 = Σ lx mx. If R0 > 1 the population grows; if R0 < 1 it shrinks.

Example: in a cohort of 100, 40 survive to age 1 and each produces 2 offspring, so R0 = (40 ÷ 100) × 2 = 0.8, below replacement.

sections.heading: Growth and regulation
sections.text:
Exponential growth assumes unlimited resources: dN/dt = rN, so Nt = N0 e^(rt). Logistic growth adds crowding: dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K), where K is the carrying capacity. Regulation is density-dependent when factors such as competition and disease intensify as N rises, and density-independent when factors such as fire and weather do not.

Example: N0 = 100, r = 0.2 per year, t = 5 years gives Nt = 100 × e^(1) = 271.8, about 272.

sections.heading: Species interactions
sections.text: Competition is the use of the same limiting resource by two species. It may be exploitative, by consuming the resource, or interference, by direct harm. It can lead to competitive exclusion or to resource partitioning. Predation is one species eating another; it can regulate prey numbers and select for defences. Mutualism benefits both partners, as when ants defend an acacia tree that supplies food and shelter.

sections.heading: Succession and biodiversity
sections.text:
Succession is directional change in community composition. Primary succession starts on bare substrate; secondary succession follows a disturbance that leaves soil. It often ends in a climax community, though disturbance can hold earlier stages. Biodiversity is measured by species richness (number of species) and evenness (relative abundance). The Shannon index is H = −Σ pi ln pi, using natural logs, where pi is the proportion of individuals in species i.

Example: two species with pi = 0.5 each give H = −(0.5 ln 0.5 + 0.5 ln 0.5) = 0.693.

keyPoints: A life table gives survivorship lx and fecundity mx; the net reproductive rate is R0 = Σ lx mx.
Exponential growth is dN/dt = rN, with Nt = N0 e^(rt).
Logistic growth is dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K), where K is carrying capacity.
Density-dependent factors regulate populations more strongly as numbers rise; density-independent factors do not.
Competition may cause competitive exclusion or resource partitioning; predation can regulate prey; mutualism benefits both partners.
Succession is directional community change; biodiversity is measured by richness, evenness and the Shannon index H = −Σ pi ln pi.

en.title: Conservation biology and wildlife management
en.short: Threats to biodiversity, extinction risk, protected areas, viability, wildlife management and planning.

sections.heading: Threats to biodiversity
sections.text: Biodiversity is the variety of genes, species and ecosystems. The main threats are habitat loss and fragmentation, overexploitation, invasive alien species, pollution and climate change. Fragmentation splits habitat into patches, reducing gene flow and increasing edge effects, where conditions near a patch edge differ from the interior. Small populations also lose genetic variation through genetic drift and inbreeding, which can lower survival and reproduction.

sections.heading: Extinction and viability
sections.text: Extinction risk is higher for species with small populations, narrow ranges, specialised needs, slow breeding or exposure to new predators. The IUCN Red List categories, from Least Concern to Extinct, are global assessments; check the current Red List because status changes. Population viability analysis (PVA) uses models to estimate the chance that a population persists over a set time. Minimum viable population is the size giving a chosen high persistence probability; estimates are uncertain. Example: 500 animals declining by 5% a year fall to 500 × 0.95^10 ≈ 299 after ten years, ignoring immigration and density effects.

sections.heading: Protected areas
sections.text: Protected areas are spaces managed mainly for conservation. Their design matters: large, well-connected reserves with corridors and buffer zones usually support more species than isolated small patches. The IUCN protected area categories range from strict nature reserve to sustainable use, but national laws differ. Wildlife management uses monitoring, harvest quotas, zoning, anti-poaching and reintroduction. Sustainable use means taking animals or plants at a rate the population can replace.

sections.heading: Conflict and planning
sections.text: Human-wildlife conflict arises when wildlife threatens safety, crops or livestock. Suppose elephants raid maize near Amina’s village. Guards, beehive fences, compensation and land-use planning can reduce losses, but local people must share in decisions and benefits. Conservation planning sets priorities from data on species, threats and costs. Systematic conservation planning selects sites to meet targets efficiently, and adaptive management monitors actions and adjusts them.

keyPoints: Main threats to biodiversity include habitat loss and fragmentation, overexploitation, invasive species, pollution and climate change.
Small populations face genetic drift and inbreeding, which raise extinction risk.
PVA estimates persistence probability; minimum viable population is a chosen persistence target, not a fixed number.
Protected areas work best when large, connected and well managed, with buffer zones and corridors.
Wildlife management includes monitoring, quotas, zoning and sustainable use within regeneration rates.
Human-wildlife conflict needs local participation, compensation and land-use planning, while conservation planning prioritises actions by threat and cost.

en.title: Evolutionary biology and phylogenetics
en.short: Microevolution, species concepts, phylogenetic methods, biogeography and coevolution.

sections.heading: Microevolution
sections.text: Microevolution is change in the frequencies of alleles (gene variants) within a population over generations. Its main causes are mutation, selection, genetic drift (random change, strongest in small populations) and gene flow (movement of alleles between populations). These processes can produce local adaptation without new species. Speciation often begins when a geographic barrier, such as a river, keeps populations apart. Reproductive isolation, meaning they can no longer interbreed even if they meet, then develops, for example through timing of breeding or courtship differences.

sections.heading: Species concepts
sections.text: A species concept is a rule for deciding whether populations belong to one species. The biological species concept defines a species as a group that interbreeds and produces fertile offspring, with reproductive isolation from other groups. It fails for asexual organisms and many plants. The morphological concept uses consistent physical differences, and the phylogenetic concept uses the smallest monophyletic group, meaning a group containing an ancestor and all its descendants. Cryptic species look alike but are genetically distinct. No single concept fits all life.

sections.heading: Phylogenetic methods
sections.text: Phylogenetics reconstructs evolutionary relationships as trees. Morphological phylogenetics uses shared derived characters (synapomorphies), while molecular phylogenetics uses DNA or protein sequences. Homology is similarity from common ancestry; analogy is similarity from convergent evolution and can mislead. An outgroup, a more distant relative used for comparison, helps root the tree. Parsimony chooses the tree with the fewest changes; likelihood and Bayesian methods use explicit models of sequence change. A tree is a hypothesis, and support values show how strongly the data favour each branch.

sections.heading: Biogeography and coevolution
sections.text: Biogeography studies why species live where they do. Vicariance is splitting of a range by a barrier, such as a new river; dispersal is movement across a barrier. For example, Amina sequences fish above and below a waterfall. If each side is monophyletic, vicariance is plausible; if one side nests inside the other, recent dispersal is more likely. Coevolution is reciprocal selection between interacting species, as in host and parasite or plant and pollinator. It can produce matching traits and ongoing arms races.

keyPoints: Microevolution is change in allele frequencies within populations, driven by mutation, selection, drift and gene flow.
Species concepts differ; the biological species concept relies on reproductive isolation and does not fit all organisms.
Phylogenetic trees are hypotheses based on shared derived characters or molecular sequence data.
Homology reflects common ancestry, while analogy reflects convergent evolution and can mislead tree building.
Biogeography explains distributions through vicariance and dispersal.
Coevolution is reciprocal selection between interacting species, such as hosts and parasites.

en.title: Molecular biology and biotechnology in zoology
en.short: DNA technologies, PCR, sequencing, cloning, CRISPR and their uses in animal science.

sections.heading: DNA tools
sections.text: Molecular biology studies DNA, RNA and proteins at the molecular level. In zoology, DNA is usually extracted from blood, tissue, hair or faeces. A primer is a short single-stranded DNA sequence that starts DNA synthesis at a chosen site. Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size using an electric field.

sections.heading: PCR and sequencing
sections.text: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) copies a target DNA region many times. Each cycle has denaturation (strand separation), primer annealing (binding) and extension by a heat-stable DNA polymerase. After about 30 cycles one copy can become over a billion, so PCR is used for diagnostics and barcoding. Sanger sequencing reads one DNA fragment at a time; next-generation sequencing reads millions in parallel. DNA barcoding sequences a standard region, such as cytochrome c oxidase subunit I (COI) in animals, and compares it with reference libraries.

sections.heading: Cloning and editing
sections.text: Cloning has two meanings. Molecular cloning puts a DNA fragment into a vector, a carrier such as a plasmid, and grows it in a host cell. Reproductive cloning makes a whole animal with the same nuclear DNA as a donor. CRISPR-Cas9 is gene editing: a guide RNA directs the Cas9 nuclease, an enzyme that cuts DNA, to a chosen DNA site. Repair of the cut can disable a gene or insert a new sequence. Off-target cuts, cuts at unintended sites, are possible, so editing must be checked.

sections.heading: Applications in zoology
sections.text: DNA methods support taxonomy, conservation, disease work and breeding. Barcoding can identify species, including cryptic species that look alike. Conservation genetics uses DNA markers, detectable sequence variations, to measure diversity and inbreeding. Molecular diagnostics, DNA-based tests, detect pathogens and identify animal vectors. Marker-assisted selection uses DNA markers linked to useful traits; transgenesis inserts foreign DNA, and its use in animals is regulated differently by country. Example: suppose Amina’s team in Kenya samples dung from a rare antelope. PCR of COI and sequencing confirm the species and show low diversity, guiding protection.

keyPoints: PCR uses thermal cycling and a heat-stable DNA polymerase to amplify a target DNA region.
Sanger sequencing reads one fragment at a time, while next-generation sequencing reads many in parallel.
DNA barcoding compares a standard region such as COI in animals with reference libraries.
Molecular cloning propagates DNA in a vector, which is different from reproductive cloning of a whole animal.
CRISPR-Cas9 uses guide RNA and Cas9 nuclease to cut DNA, and off-target effects must be checked.
Applications include taxonomy, conservation genetics, molecular diagnostics and marker-assisted breeding, with rules varying by country.

en.title: Field zoology and research methods
en.short: Sampling, trapping, transects, mark-recapture, biodiversity surveys, permits, data recording and scientific writing.

sections.heading: Planning and sampling
sections.text: Field zoology starts with a clear question and sampling design. Define the target population, the sampling unit and the effort. Random or stratified random placement reduces bias; a pilot survey tests methods. Record habitat, date, time, weather and observer. A biodiversity survey estimates species richness and relative abundance, not just a species list. Sampling may be direct observation, signs, traps, nets or acoustic recorders, but each method detects only some species.

sections.heading: Trapping and transects
sections.text: Traps must suit the animal and be checked often. Pitfall traps catch ground invertebrates; live traps and mist nets need trained handlers and quick release of non-target animals. A transect is a line or strip across a site. In a line transect, observers record animals and their distance from the line; in a belt transect, they record all animals within a fixed width. Transects are placed randomly or along gradients, and effort is reported so results can be compared.

sections.heading: Mark-recapture
sections.text: Mark-recapture estimates population size when animals are caught, marked, released and later recaught. The Lincoln-Petersen estimate is N ≈ (M × C) ÷ R, where M is the number marked first, C the number caught second and R the number of marked recaptures. Example: M = 40, C = 50, R = 8, so N ≈ (40 × 50) ÷ 8 = 250. It assumes a closed population, equal catchability, no mark loss and no births, deaths or migration between samples. If R is zero, no estimate is possible.

sections.heading: Records, ethics and writing
sections.text: Field ethics means reducing stress and non-target catch, using trained staff, releasing animals promptly and respecting local people and habitats. Collecting and research permits are often required; rules differ, so check the national wildlife authority and your institution’s animal ethics committee before fieldwork. Record raw data in a bound notebook or secure file, with units, coordinates and metadata. Back up data. Scientific writing reports methods and effort honestly, usually as introduction, methods, results and discussion, with sources cited and uncertainty stated.

keyPoints: Lincoln-Petersen estimate: N ≈ (M × C) ÷ R, assuming a closed population and equal catchability.
Random or stratified sampling reduces bias, and effort must be recorded.
Traps must suit the target animal and be checked often; release non-target animals promptly.
Biodiversity surveys estimate species richness and relative abundance; line and belt transects are common designs.
Check national wildlife and animal ethics permits before fieldwork; rules vary by country.
Record raw data with units, coordinates, date and observer, back up files, and report methods and uncertainty honestly.

en.title: Fisheries and aquaculture
en.short: Fish biology applied to capture fisheries, stock assessment, pond and cage culture, nutrition and disease.

sections.heading: Fish biology and stocks
sections.text: A fishery is a fish population exploited by people, together with the fishing activity and area. Capture fisheries take wild fish; aquaculture farms aquatic organisms under controlled or partly controlled conditions. Most fish are ectotherms, so temperature sets metabolism, growth and oxygen demand. Gills take dissolved oxygen, and water quality limits stocking. Growth, maturity and recruitment, the entry of young fish into the exploited stock, link biology to management. A stock is the unit assessed and managed, often a breeding population in a defined area.

sections.heading: Stock assessment
sections.text:
