Stock assessment estimates abundance and predicts how fishing changes it. In a simple model, numbers decline exponentially: N_t = N_0 × e^(−Zt), where Z is total mortality and t is time. Z = F + M, with F fishing mortality and M natural mortality. High F reduces future spawning biomass.

Example: N_0 = 10,000 and Z = 0.5 per year. After one year N_1 = 10,000 × e^(−0.5) = 10,000 × 0.6065 = 6,065 fish. Real assessments use catch, age, length and survey data. Maximum sustainable yield is a reference concept, not a fixed number.

sections.heading: Pond and cage culture
sections.text: Pond culture uses enclosed ponds, often fertilised to grow natural food and supplemented with feed. Stocking is limited by dissolved oxygen, ammonia and temperature; aeration and water exchange raise carrying capacity. Cage culture holds fish in nets in lakes, rivers or the sea. Water flows through, supplying oxygen, but waste, escapes and disease transfer are risks. Site selection and carrying capacity matter.

sections.heading: Nutrition, disease and sustainability
sections.text: Feeds must supply protein with essential amino acids, energy, lipids, vitamins and minerals. Feed conversion ratio (FCR) = feed given ÷ live weight gain; a lower FCR means more efficient use. Stress from crowding or poor water quality predisposes fish to disease. Biosecurity, vaccination, quarantine and good husbandry reduce losses. Sustainability requires managing overfishing, bycatch, habitat damage, feed fishmeal and nutrient pollution. Rules differ by country, so check current national fisheries and aquaculture regulations.

keyPoints: Capture fisheries exploit wild stocks; aquaculture farms aquatic organisms.
Most fish are ectotherms, so temperature and dissolved oxygen limit growth and stocking density.
Total mortality is Z = F + M, and numbers decline as N_t = N_0 × e^(−Zt).
Feed conversion ratio is FCR = feed given ÷ live weight gain.
Pond and cage culture differ in water exchange, waste and escape risk.
Sustainability needs limits on fishing, bycatch, pollution and feed use, and rules vary by country.

en.title: Professional practice, ethics and animal welfare in zoology
en.short: Animal ethics and welfare, biosafety, research integrity, wildlife and laboratory rules, and zoologist duties.

sections.heading: Ethics and welfare
sections.text: Animal ethics asks whether animal use is justified and how to limit harm. Animal welfare is the animal’s state, judged by health, behaviour and stress. The Five Freedoms cover hunger and thirst, discomfort, pain, injury and disease, fear and distress, and normal behaviour. In research, the 3Rs are replacement, reduction and refinement: avoid animals where possible, use fewer, and lessen suffering. A protocol states purpose, species, numbers, procedures, anaesthesia, analgesia and a humane endpoint, the planned point for ending an animal’s involvement to prevent suffering.

sections.heading: Biosafety and integrity
sections.text: Biosafety means working so biological agents do not harm people, animals or the environment. It starts with risk assessment, then containment, protective clothing, disinfection, waste and transport. Field work adds zoonoses, infections passed from animals to people, and biosecurity to avoid moving invasive species or pathogens. Research integrity means honesty in design, data, analysis and reporting. Fabrication, falsification and plagiarism are misconduct. Keep data, record methods, agree authorship, declare conflicts and report errors. Ethics approval does not replace responsibility.

sections.heading: Regulation and permits
sections.text: Legal requirements vary by country and often by state. Laboratory animal use may need approval from an institutional animal care and use committee, trained staff, veterinary care and records. Wildlife work may need permits for capture, handling, sampling, transport or keeping specimens, especially protected species. In Nigeria, national and state wildlife laws apply, and details change; check current official sources. International rules also matter, such as the Nagoya Protocol on access to genetic resources and benefit sharing. A permit from one country does not cover another.

sections.heading: Responsibilities in practice
sections.text: Responsibilities include competence, consent from landowners, minimal disturbance and honest reporting. Case: Amina, a student in Kano, plans to trap rodents near farms. She needs supervisor approval, ethics review, landowner and wildlife authority permission, a zoonosis risk assessment, gloves, disinfection, traps and a humane endpoint. She records animals, releases non-target species and stores data. If conditions cannot be met, she changes the plan or stops.

keyPoints: Animal welfare is assessed from health, behaviour and stress, not from human intention alone.
The 3Rs are replacement, reduction and refinement of animal use.
Biosafety begins with risk assessment and includes containment, protective clothing, disinfection and safe waste.
Research integrity requires honest data, methods, authorship and reporting; fabrication, falsification and plagiarism are misconduct.
Laboratory and wildlife work usually need ethics approval and permits, but the exact rules vary by country and state.
Zoologists must obtain consent, minimise disturbance, protect data and stop work if welfare or legal conditions cannot be met.

en.title: Advanced evolutionary genetics and genomics
en.short: Population genetics, molecular evolution, phylogenomics and adaptation genomics in animals.

sections.heading: Variation and drift
sections.text:
An allele’s frequency is p; with two alleles p + q = 1. Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium predicts genotype frequencies p², 2pq and q² when mating is random, the population is large, and selection, mutation and migration are absent.

Example: p = 0.6 and q = 0.4 give AA = 0.36, Aa = 0.48 and aa = 0.16, which sum to 1.00.

Drift is random change in frequency, strongest in small populations. Effective population size (Ne) is the size of an ideal population with the same drift; it is usually far below the census count.

sections.heading: Molecular evolution
sections.text: Molecular evolution compares sequences. Synonymous substitutions do not change the amino acid; nonsynonymous ones do. The ratio dN/dS (also written Ka/Ks) near 1 suggests neutrality, well below 1 purifying selection, above 1 positive selection. The molecular clock assumes substitutions accumulate at a roughly steady rate, giving approximate divergence times, but rates vary between genes and lineages, so dates need fossil calibration.

sections.heading: Phylogenomics
sections.text: Phylogenomics builds trees from many loci. Orthologues descend from one ancestral gene by speciation; paralogues arise by duplication and can mislead. Concatenation joins loci into one alignment. Coalescent methods model each gene tree and allow for incomplete lineage sorting, where ancestral variants persist so gene trees differ from the species tree. Support comes from bootstrapping or posterior probabilities.

sections.heading: Adaptation genomics
sections.text: Adaptation genomics searches for loci under selection. Genome scans compare Fst, the share of variation between populations, across loci and flag outliers; environmental association and common-garden experiments then test function. Genome-wide association studies link genotype to phenotype. Raw reads are quality-checked, assembled and annotated. Reference-genome bias and small samples are common pitfalls.

keyPoints: Hardy-Weinberg: p + q = 1 and genotype frequencies are p², 2pq and q².
Drift is strongest in small populations; Ne measures its strength.
dN/dS near 1 means neutrality, below 1 purifying selection, above 1 positive selection.
Molecular clock dates are approximate and need fossil calibration.
Orthologues are speciation copies, paralogues duplication copies; only orthologues compare like with like.
Incomplete lineage sorting makes gene trees differ from the species tree.

en.title: Molecular ecology and conservation genetics
en.short: eDNA, population structure, gene flow, parentage, conservation units and genetic monitoring.

sections.heading: Environmental DNA
sections.text: Environmental DNA (eDNA) is genetic material shed into water, soil or sediment. Samples are filtered or extracted, then DNA is amplified by qPCR (quantitative PCR) for one species or by metabarcoding, where many short barcode regions are sequenced and matched to reference libraries. eDNA finds rare animals without capture but does not measure abundance directly. DNA moves and degrades, so field blanks and negative controls are essential. A positive result means DNA is present, not a live animal at that spot. Reference databases are incomplete for many tropical taxa.

sections.heading: Structure and gene flow
sections.text:
Population genetic structure is the non-random distribution of allele frequencies among populations. Gene flow is allele movement between populations through migration and reproduction. F-statistics compare diversity within and among populations. FST = (HT − HS) ÷ HT, where HS is mean expected heterozygosity within subpopulations and HT is expected heterozygosity of the total population. FST near 0 means little differentiation; near 1 means strong differentiation.

Example: two populations, allele A frequency 0.8 and 0.4.
Mean p = 0.6.
HS = (2×0.8×0.2 + 2×0.4×0.6) ÷ 2 = 0.40.
HT = 2×0.6×0.4 = 0.48.
FST = (0.48 − 0.40) ÷ 0.48 = 0.17.

sections.heading: Parentage and units
sections.text: Parentage analysis assigns offspring to parents using Mendelian inheritance. It uses exclusion, where incompatible parents are removed, or likelihood methods that compare candidate pedigrees. Markers include microsatellites and single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Relatedness estimators use shared alleles to estimate how closely individuals are related. A conservation unit is a population managed as a distinct group. An evolutionarily significant unit (ESU) usually shows deep genetic divergence and reproductive isolation; a management unit (MU) is demographically independent but not necessarily reproductively isolated. Legal definitions vary by country.

sections.heading: Genetic monitoring
sections.text: Genetic monitoring is repeated sampling to track diversity, effective population size (Ne), inbreeding and introgression. Ne is the size of an ideal population that would lose diversity at the same rate; it is smaller than the census count. Monitoring guides translocations and captive breeding. It needs consistent markers and archived samples. One survey cannot show a trend; two comparable time points are needed.

keyPoints: eDNA detects DNA shed into the environment; field blanks and negative controls are essential because DNA moves and degrades.
FST = (HT − HS) ÷ HT measures differentiation; HS is mean expected heterozygosity within subpopulations and HT is expected heterozygosity of the total population.
Gene flow is allele movement between populations through migration and reproduction.
Parentage is assigned by exclusion or likelihood methods using markers such as microsatellites and SNPs.
Conservation units include evolutionarily significant units (ESUs) and management units (MUs); legal definitions vary by country.
Genetic monitoring tracks effective population size (Ne), diversity and introgression over repeated samples.

en.title: Advanced animal physiology and ecophysiology
en.short: Comparative responses to temperature, water, oxygen and stress, with metabolic ecology and environmental change.

sections.heading: Temperature and metabolism
sections.text:
Ecophysiology studies how physiological traits respond to the environment and affect survival and reproduction. Phenotypic plasticity is the ability of one genotype to produce different phenotypes. Acclimation is reversible adjustment by an individual, such as heat hardening; adaptation is heritable change across generations. Thermal tolerance is often summarised by CTmax and CTmin, the upper and lower temperatures at which performance collapses.

The Q10 coefficient compares rates at two temperatures: Q10 = (R2 ÷ R1)^(10 ÷ (T2 − T1)). If R1 = 40 at 20°C and R2 = 80 at 30°C, Q10 = (80 ÷ 40)^(10 ÷ 10) = 2.0, so the rate doubles over that 10°C rise.

sections.heading: Water and ions
sections.text: Water balance depends on osmolarity, the total solute concentration. Osmoconformers let body osmolarity follow the environment; osmoregulators keep it stable using ion transport, kidneys or glands. Euryhaline animals tolerate wide salinity; stenohaline animals do not. In dry habitats, water loss is reduced by behaviour, low-permeability surfaces and concentrated urine. These responses cost energy, so they trade off against growth and reproduction.

sections.heading: Oxygen and stress
sections.text: Hypoxia is low oxygen availability. Aerobic scope is the difference between maximum and resting aerobic metabolism. Many animals regulate oxygen uptake until a critical oxygen tension, below which uptake falls. Stress is a disturbance that threatens homeostasis; allostasis is the active adjustment that keeps function stable. Heat shock proteins help protect proteins during heat or other stress, while glucocorticoids can mobilise energy but may suppress growth if chronic.

sections.heading: Metabolic ecology and change
sections.text: Metabolic ecology links metabolism to ecology. Basal or standard metabolic rate is the minimum cost of maintenance. Metabolic rate usually scales with body mass as R = aM^b; b is often near 3/4 across species but varies. The metabolic theory of ecology uses this scaling to predict ecological rates. Under environmental change, populations may shift range, acclimate, or evolve. Because plasticity has limits, predicting winners requires measuring tolerance, performance curves and energy budgets, not temperature alone.

keyPoints: Ecophysiology links physiological traits to environmental conditions and fitness.
Acclimation is reversible within an individual; adaptation is heritable across generations.
Q10 = (R2 ÷ R1)^(10 ÷ (T2 − T1)); a Q10 of 2 means the rate doubles for a 10°C rise.
Osmoconformers match body osmolarity to the environment, while osmoregulators maintain it.
Hypoxia reduces aerobic scope; critical oxygen tension marks the point where oxygen uptake falls.
Metabolic rate scales with body mass as R = aM^b, with b often near 3/4 but variable.

en.title: Research methods and dissertation in zoology
en.short: Proposals, literature review, field and lab design, statistics, ethics, data management and thesis writing.

sections.heading: Proposal and review
sections.text: A research proposal states a clear question, testable hypotheses, aims, methods, timeline, budget and risks. It should show that the study is feasible and that the question fills a gap. A literature review is not a list of papers: define search terms and inclusion criteria, assess study quality, and synthesise what is known and unknown. Record the search so it can be repeated. This review shapes the question and prevents unnecessary duplication.

sections.heading: Design and statistics
sections.text: Experimental design needs controls, replication, randomisation and, where possible, blocking to reduce confounding. Field design must match sampling to the animal’s scale and detectability; pilot studies test logistics. Advanced statistics begins with the unit of replication. If Amina samples 12 ponds three times, she has 36 observations but only 12 independent units; treating visits as independent is pseudoreplication. Use mixed-effects models with pond as a random effect, and check assumptions. Report effect sizes and confidence intervals, not only p values. A power analysis before sampling estimates how many independent units are needed.

sections.heading: Ethics and data
sections.text: Research ethics covers animal welfare, permits, consent and honesty. Animal work needs ethics approval and, in many countries, a licence; follow the 3Rs (replacement, reduction, refinement) and humane endpoints, pre-agreed signs that end a procedure to prevent suffering. Fieldwork needs landowner and wildlife permits. A data management plan names file formats, metadata, storage, backup, access and retention. Use version control and unique identifiers. Keep raw data unchanged and document every cleaning step. Sharing data should respect privacy, community agreements and national rules.

sections.heading: Writing and defence
sections.text: A thesis is an argument, not a diary. Most zoology theses use the IMRaD pattern: introduction, methods, results and discussion, plus a general abstract and references. Write each chapter around one question, present results without interpretation, then discuss meaning, limitations and alternative explanations. Keep a clear audit trail from raw data to figures. The viva examines whether you understand your choices. Rehearse concise answers about design, statistics and ethics.

keyPoints: A proposal must state a testable question, feasible methods and a clear gap.
A literature review uses explicit search and inclusion criteria and synthesises evidence.
Good design uses controls, replication, randomisation and blocking where appropriate.
Pseudoreplication treats repeated measurements as independent; mixed models can account for grouping.
Ethics approval, permits, the 3Rs and humane endpoints are required for animal research.
A data management plan and an audit trail make thesis work reproducible and defensible.
